messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David sits in the chair with the stillness of a man trying not to disturb the air around him. At thirty, his carpenter’s hands, usually steady and capable, rest uncertainly on his knees. The story of the last eight months doesn’t come easily; for him, the event isn't a narrative he can recount but a physical state he falls back into. He explains that he can’t seem to put the frightening parts into words, that they exist as a knot of sensation just below his throat. It began on a Tuesday at a residential job site. He was on a short break, leaning against a stack of lumber and sipping a hot, sweet hazelnut coffee from a thermos, when he heard the shout, followed by a sickening thud. His friend and colleague, Marco, had fallen from the second-story scaffolding.

David was the first one there. The memory, when it comes for him now, is never a simple recollection. It arrives without warning, a complete sensory ambush. He’ll be at home and his wife, Sarah, will gently touch his arm, and suddenly it is no longer her hand but the horrifyingly slick, warm feeling of Marco’s blood on his own as he tried to apply pressure to the wound on his leg. The sight of the exposed bone, stark white against the crimson, is an image that can flash into his mind if he sees so much as a child with a scraped knee at the park. When these moments hit, it feels completely real. He’s back on the dusty ground, the smell of sawdust in the air, the cloying taste of hazelnut coffee still coating his tongue as he tries not to be sick. The world of his living room dissolves, replaced by the full, terrifying reality of that moment.

In the weeks that followed the accident, David began to change. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally broken, that the trauma had permanently altered him for the worse. This certainty settled deep inside him, colouring every interaction. He stopped drinking coffee entirely, the taste now a potent trigger. He began flinching from Sarah’s touch, pulling away from the very comfort he needed, because any physical contact could send him spiraling. Confused and hurt, she started keeping her distance, and a quiet chasm opened between them. At work, he became a liability. A coworker nicked his hand with a utility knife, and the sight of the small beads of blood sent David into a state of near-paralysis. He just stood there, staring, until his foreman shook him and sent him home. He started deliberately trying to make his mind go blank when he felt a memory approaching, staring fixedly at a point on the wall until the world fuzzed out at the edges, a strategy that left him feeling even more disconnected.

The conviction that he could no longer rely on himself became absolute. He, who had always been so dependable, now felt like a stranger in his own body. To manage the constant, thrumming anxiety, he began to eat. At night, long after Sarah was asleep, he would go to the kitchen and consume food without tasting it—a whole box of cereal, a bag of chips, anything to fill the gnawing emptiness and quiet the noise in his head. He avoided talking or even thinking about what happened, believing that if he just pushed it down hard enough, it might eventually stay buried. But this only seemed to give the memories more power when they inevitably broke through. He felt as though his life, the one he had carefully built with his hands and his heart, had been completely destroyed. The capable man, the loving husband, was gone, replaced by this fragile, frightened shell. It was Sarah who finally brought him here. Last week, after he recoiled from her attempt at a hug, she had looked at him with tears in her eyes and said, “I miss you, David. I don’t know where you’ve gone.” He is here now because he is terrified that she is right, and that he will never find his way back.
